5. Views and Widgets

Describe in general the purpose and basic characteristics of:

5. Views and Widgets

Describe the purpose and basic characteristics of these Android widgets: TextView, EditText, Button, ImageView, Spinner, CheckBox, RadioButton and RadioGroup, DatePicker, AnalogClock and TextClock, VideoView, ViewPager, and ProgressBar.
android-midterm-2026-036.backText:
The following twelve cards cover the widgets in this bullet’s list: TextView, EditText, Button, ImageView, Spinner, CheckBox, RadioButton/RadioGroup, DatePicker, AnalogClock/TextClock, VideoView, ViewPager, and ProgressBar.

For each, be able to say what it displays or accepts, how the user interacts with it, and the important property or method illustrated by the lecture. The individual cards include relevant examples.

Slides: 7, pp. 7–111; 11, p. 87; 12, p. 75. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-055.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

Be able to describe the main principles governing placement of Views in:
android-midterm-2026-055.backText:
• LinearLayout: places children sequentially in one horizontal row or vertical column.
  • FrameLayout: places children in a shared area, potentially overlapping/stacked.
  • TableLayout: organizes children into rows and columns using TableRows.
  • ConstraintLayout: positions/sizes children using relationships to the parent and other Views.

The next four cards cover the rules and key attributes for each layout.

Slides: 11, pp. 24–56, 88–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Be able to understand and describe basic navigational patterns

8. Navigational patterns

Describe these navigational patterns: target navigation (lateral, descendant, ancestral), swipe views, tabs, navigation drawer, master/detail flow, action bar, menus and action buttons, Floating Action Button, and dialogs.
backText:
The review lists target navigation, swipe views, tabs, navigation drawer, master/detail flow, action bar/menus/action buttons, Floating Action Button, and dialogs. The following eight cards define each of those patterns.

The supplied fragment examples substantively demonstrate master/detail flow. Most other patterns are absent or only mentioned, so their individual cards mark supplemental material.

Slides: 8, pp. 65–69; 12, pp. 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

Source note: The slides demonstrate master/detail flow. The other descriptions below are supplemental summaries of the existing individual cards because those patterns are absent or only mentioned in the supplied slides.

  • Target navigation: Lateral moves between sibling destinations; descendant moves deeper, such as list to item details; ancestral moves toward a parent, such as details to the containing list.
  • Swipe views: Move between adjacent sibling pages using a swipe gesture, commonly through ViewPager.
  • Tabs: Visible labels select sibling pages and indicate the current page; they can be paired with swipe views.
  • Navigation drawer: A panel listing major app destinations, opened from a menu icon or edge gesture.
  • Master/detail flow: A list (master) leads to details for the selected item. The slides show separate portrait screens and side-by-side landscape fragments; retain the selected list index across rotation.
  • Action bar, menus and action buttons: The top app bar shows a title, navigation controls, and actions. Menus define commands; action buttons expose common commands and an overflow menu holds others.
  • Floating Action Button: A prominent floating button for the main action on a screen, such as adding an item.
  • Dialogs: Focused overlays for a short decision, alert, or input task, then dismissal returns to the underlying screen.

Slides: 8, pp. 65–69; 12, pp. 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-061.frontText:
6. Layouts and View positioning

For each of the above layouts, be able to name principal XML attributes and provide their meaning.
android-midterm-2026-061.backText:
• LinearLayout: orientation (row/column), gravity (alignment of contents), child layout_gravity (child alignment), layout_weight (share of remaining space), weightSum (specified total weight).
  • FrameLayout: child layout_gravity (placement), foreground (drawable overlay), foregroundGravity (foreground alignment), measureAllChildren (whether all children are measured, including gone children).
  • TableLayout: stretchColumns, shrinkColumns, collapseColumns (column behavior); child layout_column (zero-based column) and layout_span (number of columns).
  • ConstraintLayout: layout_constraintStart_toStartOf / End_toEndOf / Top_toTopOf / Top_toBottomOf (edge relationships), layout_constraintHorizontal_bias / Vertical_bias (placement between opposing constraints), layout_constraintHorizontal_chainStyle (chain distribution). Constraint attributes use the app prefix.

Dimensions and margins are child layout parameters as well. Match the attribute to the layout class: layout_weight belongs to LinearLayout; constraint relationships belong to ConstraintLayout.

Slides: 11, pp. 25–38, 46–55, 93–119. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-075.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Carefully review chapter 10 and lecture slides on eLC
android-midterm-2026-075.backText:
The supplied slides cover Up/parent Activity declarations in Lecture 8, pp. 65–69 and master/detail fragment arrangements in Lecture 12, pp. 24–39 and 65–69. No dedicated navigation lecture is present in the supplied folder.

The cards for the remaining navigation patterns explicitly label explanations added to fill those gaps. They cover only the navigation bullets requested in the review; no textbook material has been added.

android-midterm-2026-076.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Distinguish between back and up navigation
android-midterm-2026-076.backText:
The slides introduce navigation and show a parent Activity relationship for Up navigation through android:parentActivityName. The earlier back-stack slides show returning to a previous Activity.

Supplemental explanation: Back follows the user’s navigation history, usually returning to the previous destination and potentially leaving the app. Up follows the app’s hierarchy to the logical parent destination. Example: if a details page is opened from outside the app, Back can return to that outside app, while Up leads to the details page’s parent inside this app. Within ordinary hierarchical navigation, the two may lead to the same place.

Slides: 8, pp. 4, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-078.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Target navigation (lateral, descendant, ancestral)
android-midterm-2026-078.backText:
The review explicitly asks for lateral, descendant, and ancestral target navigation. A detailed definition of these three terms was not found in the supplied slides.

Supplemental explanation: Lateral: move between destinations at the same level, such as sibling sections selected by tabs. Descendant: move deeper into the hierarchy, such as a list → an item’s details. Ancestral: move toward a parent/ancestor, such as details → its containing list. Classify the relationship between the source and destination, rather than the visual direction of an animation.

Slides: 8, pp. 65–69 (general navigation introduction). PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-079.backText:
Paging fragments is mentioned in the slides, but swipe-view navigation is not developed into a full example.

Supplemental explanation: Swipe views let the user move between adjacent pages with a swipe gesture, commonly through a ViewPager. They fit sibling content at the same level. Provide an indication of the current page, such as tabs or a page indicator; a swipe changes pages rather than scrolling the content vertically.

Slides: 12, p. 75; 11, p. 87. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-080.backText:
A substantive tabs explanation was not found in the supplied slides.

Supplemental explanation: Tabs expose a small group of sibling sections/pages with visible labels. Selecting a tab switches to that section; the selected tab indicates the current one. Tabs can be paired with swipe views, so tapping a tab or swiping changes the same current page. Moving between these sibling pages is lateral navigation.

Slides: 8, pp. 65–69 (general navigation introduction). PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-081.backText:
A substantive navigation-drawer explanation was not found in the supplied slides.

Supplemental explanation: A navigation drawer is a panel, commonly opened from a menu icon or edge gesture, that lists major app destinations. Selecting an item navigates to that section. It is useful when several main destinations should be reachable from a shared navigation menu, while the panel can stay closed during content viewing.

Slides: 8, pp. 65–69 (general navigation introduction). PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-082.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Master detail flow
android-midterm-2026-082.backText:
Master/detail flow starts with a list of items (master) and shows information about the selected item (detail). The fragment slides directly demonstrate this pattern.

  • Portrait/narrow: the list and details appear on separate screens/Activities.
  • Landscape/wide: the list and detail fragments can appear side by side inside one Activity.
  • State: retain the selected item’s list index and use it to restore the matching details when orientation changes.

The UGA information example and AndroidVersionsFragments reuse the same list/details logic across the two arrangements. The list-index selection is the connection between the master selection and the displayed detail.

Slides: 12, pp. 24–39, 46–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-083.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Action bar, Menus, and Action Buttons
android-midterm-2026-083.backText:
The slides contain limited ActionBar context, but do not fully explain the action bar/menu/action-button pattern.

Supplemental explanation: The action bar / app bar is the top area that can show the screen title, navigation affordances, and actions. A menu defines the available commands; common commands can appear as visible action buttons, while other commands appear in an overflow menu. An action button performs a command, such as search or save; an Up button in the bar navigates to the logical parent.

Slides: 7 (limited ActionBar examples); 8, pp. 65–69 (navigation context). PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-084.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Navigational pattern

Floating Action Button
android-midterm-2026-084.backText:
A substantive Floating Action Button explanation was not found in the supplied slides.

Supplemental explanation: A Floating Action Button (FAB) is a prominent floating button used for a primary action on the current screen, such as adding an item or composing a message. Its emphasis makes the main action easy to find. It triggers an action; it is not a menu containing all of the app’s destinations.

Slides: No substantive coverage in the supplied ten decks. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-085.backText:
DialogFragment is named among fragment types, and an Activity lifecycle example shows a dialog briefly interrupting interaction. A full navigation-pattern explanation of dialogs is not provided.

Supplemental explanation: A dialog is a focused overlay for a short decision, alert, or input task, such as confirming deletion. It temporarily interrupts interaction with the underlying screen and then dismisses back to that context. DialogFragment hosts a dialog using fragment lifecycle management. A dialog is useful for a small focused task rather than a whole major app section.

Slides: 12, p. 40; 6, pp. 65–72. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.

android-midterm-2026-086.frontText:
8. Navigational patterns

Explain how a single activity application works
android-midterm-2026-086.backText:
The slides show Activities hosting and replacing Fragments through FragmentManager/FragmentTransactions, including a landscape Activity with both list and detail fragments.

Supplemental explanation: A single-Activity application uses one Activity as the host for multiple destinations, commonly represented by Fragments. Navigation changes the fragment(s) displayed in a container rather than starting a new Activity for every screen. The host and fragment manager coordinate transitions; reversible fragment transactions can be added to a back stack so Back returns to the previous fragment destination. This is a general explanation built from the hosting/transaction concepts; the supplied slides do not provide a dedicated single-Activity navigation architecture lesson.

Slides: 12, pp. 3–20, 24–39, 65–69. PDF page numbers count the cover as page 1. Code examples are practice adaptations of the slide concepts.
